turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I've done his obs before you call him. Blood pressure was one forty two over ninety, no, hang on, I rechecked it, one thirty six over eighty four. Pulse seventy six beats a minute, and the finger-prick was eleven point four millimoles.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely, leave those up. Can you stay a minute? I want the prescription screen when we get to the insulin.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): It's already up. Lantus, twenty four units at night, and metformin on the repeats. He's been waiting about twenty minutes, bit fidgety.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alan, in you come. Park yourself. What's brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. The sugars are up, I think, and I'm just tired all the time. Properly washed out.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long's the tiredness been going on?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, a fortnight. No, more like six weeks. Maybe longer than that, I don't know.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): And at home, what numbers is the meter actually showing?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Fasting was one-eighty-something. Or one-sixty, I looked this morning and it's gone out of my head. I don't know, doctor, the meter's by the kettle.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll ignore that, then. A muddled one-eighty-something isn't a number I can use. Thirsty at all? Up in the night weeing?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Thirsty, yes, quite a bit. Weeing more as well, I suppose. When it started, I don't know.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight coming off?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No. If anything the trousers are tighter. I don't know, doctor, I haven't been on the scales.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain? Short of breath?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I can do the stairs.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me the metformin as you take it, not as the box might say.
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Five hundred milligrams. No, sorry, the big ones, a gram by mouth, twice a day with food, for the diabetes. Those I do take.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the night-time insulin?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Lantus. Eighteen units, at night, for the sugars. I think that's what I dial. I don't know, doctor, the pen all looks the same.
[SEG0020] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry, the repeat that's been issued says twenty four units of Lantus once a night. Has done for months.
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Twenty four? I don't do twenty four. I stop at eighteen. Unless I've been reading the dial wrong in the dark.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): So one of you has eighteen and the screen has twenty four, and I am not going to pretend I know which is right sitting here.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Doesn't matter some nights anyway. On work days I skip it. Early start at the warehouse, I don't fancy going hypo on the bus.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Roughly how many nights a week does that happen?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Three. Maybe four. Depends on the rota, I lose track.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. So whatever the number on the pen, it isn't going in every night. That's the bit that worries me.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): My brother says just copy him. He's on metformin too, only five hundred. And my sister, she's mad on her biotin for her nails, keeps leaving the bottle on my table.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your brother's metformin is his, and your sister's biotin is hers. Neither of those is a plan for you. Don't start the biotin, and don't cut your dose to match him.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Dad had the diabetes as well, type two. My brother's got it too. So, you know.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many years have you been diagnosed?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Seven years. Actually eight. They picked it up when I turned fifty, and I'm fifty eight now.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else you've been on? Gliclazide, empagliflozin, anything stopped?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Gliclazide they stopped when the insulin began. I don't take it now. It was eighty milligrams, I think. I don't know.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stopped, noted. I'll put eighty milligrams as you remember it, but I'm not treating that as gospel.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of. Penicillin gave my brother a rash years back, but I've had antibiotics fine. That's his problem.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Feet. Numbness, burning, any sores you've spotted?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): A bit of tingling in the toes at night. Not burning. No sores. I don't know if tingling even counts.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Both feet, or one?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Mostly the left. I think. I don't know, doctor. It's not every night.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Eye screening, the camera photos. When was the last one?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know. Could've been last year. Could've been the year before. I never kept the letter.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blurring, floaters, trouble with reading?
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Eyes feel alright. I can read the paper if I find my glasses, and those are just age.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Glasses we'll leave. Socks off, I'll have a look.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Left one's got a hole in the heel. I keep meaning to get to the shop. Sorry about that.

[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Skin's intact both sides, no ulcers, nothing between the toes. Pulses are present, both feet. Monofilament is a bit dull on the left big toe, and the right foot feels it normally.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): Is the left one bad, then?
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): It might be early nerve change from the sugar, or it might just be the way you were sitting on that chair. I am not going to call it neuropathy today. Not for certain.

[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): As for the sugars, it could be the nights you skip, or you really are only on eighteen and the record's wrong, or the early shifts. I will not decide between those until a fresh HbA1c is back. Working impression, provisionally, is type two that's not well controlled, most likely the missed insulin.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): So what am I meant to do? I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay on the metformin, a gram twice a day, no change. Do not fiddle the insulin dose tonight. Bring the pen and the box next time so we can read the dial and the label together.
[SEG0053] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can sort bloods if you want them. HbA1c, kidney function, and a urine pot for the albumin ratio. Phlebotomy's still open.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, arrange all three today, please. That's the plan, not a maybe.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Do I starve? I never know with blood tests.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): No need. Eat something. On work mornings have toast at least. Going in empty and skipping the insulin is a bad mix, and I'm saying that as advice, not a lecture.
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Feet, have a look every evening. Any break in the skin, any sore, ring the surgery the same day. If you spot a sore, don't wait for me to see you.
[SEG0058] person_3 (PATIENT): What about the eyes, then? I still don't know when I went.
[SEG0059] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book the retinal screening yourself with the service. I'll mention it in the note, but the appointment won't appear unless you ring them.
[SEG0060] person_3 (PATIENT): Alright. And coming back here?
[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you in four weeks with the results. If the sugars are making you feel properly ill before that, or you're vomiting, come back sooner, don't sit on it.
[SEG0062] person_3 (PATIENT): Four weeks. The rota's a pain but I'll swap a shift. Thanks. I think.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

bad.reason: Patient says he can read the paper if he finds his glasses.
Doctor says right foot feels monofilament normally, not absent.
bad.text: Monofilament felt normally (body_site=right foot, status=absent, observed_by=doctor)

omissions.text: Night-time insulin adherence detail: patient said he skips Lantus on work days because he is worried about going hypo on the bus.
Doctor specifically advised not to start biotin and not to cut his metformin dose to match his brother's 500 mg dose.
Patient reported no numbness in the feet when specifically asked about numbness, burning, or sores.
Retinal screening timing is unknown: patient said last screening could have been last year or the year before and he did not keep the letter.
Doctor said no fasting was needed for the blood tests.
